title: Boat and Helicopter Tourism
desc: Plan a small boat or helicopter tour offering with safe operations, licences, weather rules, guest care and pricing.
outcomes: Explain operator duties and passenger safety.
Compute cost per hour and per guest.
task: Plan a tour product with route, safety briefing, weather rules, licences, price and incident plan, working with licensed operators.
condition: A computer, a map, a spreadsheet, two peers and a licensed operator mentor. Learners do not operate vessels or aircraft.
standard: Licences and insurance are checked with sources; weather go/no-go rules are written; briefing covers equipment and emergencies; cost per guest is correct; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Tour planners, guides, hotel desks, port staff.
evidence: route plan, briefing script, go/no-go rules, price sheet
modules: Designing the tour product
Understand
A tour is a product: a route, a time, a promise and a safety plan. Design all four before selling a single seat.
Types: scenic loops, sunset trips, wildlife viewing, island transfers and special-occasion flights.
Fix duration, number of guests, boarding point, landing or mooring point and toilet or rest access.
Plan accessibility: step-free boarding, help for older guests and children, seat limits.
Add a weather back-up: a shorter route, a new date or an indoor alternative.
A 45-minute coastal route has a 20-minute boarding window, 8 guests, a sunset slot in season and a harbour museum visit as the rainy-day alternative.
Design a route with a map, timings, capacity, accessibility notes and a weather alternative.
Route has times, capacity, access notes and a backup plan.
Licences, certificates and insurance
Apply
Only licensed operators, qualified crews and certified vessels or aircraft carry paying guests.
Check vessel or aircraft certificates, crew licences and operator permits with the authority.
Confirm passenger insurance and its limits in writing.
Write down expiry dates and set reminders one month ahead.
If the operator is a partner, you still check; you cannot hand off your duty to guests.
A tour desk finds that a boat certificate expires on 30 November. It stops selling trips after that date until the new certificate is shown.
Build a licence and insurance checklist with source and expiry date for each item.
Every item has an authority, document number or practice placeholder and a date.
Weather rules and go/no-go decisions
Apply
Safety beats schedule. Rules must be written before the day, with numbers.
Choose limits: wind speed, wave height, visibility, cloud ceiling and temperature.
Use two forecast sources and a rule for when they disagree: follow the cautious one.
Name one decision maker with authority to cancel and record each decision.
Plan the guest message: reason, new date or refund, and a thank-you.
The rule says: no trip if wind exceeds 20 knots or visibility is under 5 km. At 07:30 the forecast shows 24 knots; the decision maker cancels and sends the message by 08:00.
Write go/no-go rules with numbers and a message template.
Rules have limits, decision maker and guest message.
Briefing and equipment
Apply
Guests who understand the rules stay safe and enjoy the trip more.
Briefing items: equipment, exits, seat belts or life jackets, behaviour and what to do in an emergency.
Use plain words, pictures and the guests' language; ask guests to repeat key steps.
Inspect equipment before each trip and log it.
Special briefing for children, older guests and guests with disabilities.
Guests repeat how to fasten a life jacket before boarding. A picture card on every seat shows the steps.
Write a briefing script under five minutes and make a picture card.
Script covers equipment, exits, behaviour and emergency, and a peer can repeat it.
Emergency planning and drills
Evaluate
Emergencies are rare, so practice is the only preparation.
Plan for man overboard or passenger emergency, fire, engine or equipment failure and medical events.
Assign roles, contacts and radio channels; keep emergency numbers visible.
Practise a drill every month and record the time to complete it.
Review each drill and change the plan.
A drill finds the radio channel on the sheet was wrong. The sheet is corrected and the next drill recovers a dummy in 90 seconds.
Write an emergency plan and run a table-top drill.
Plan has roles, contacts and drill results.
Costs, price and break-even
Analyse
Tours are expensive to run; price must cover real costs.
Costs: crew, fuel, maintenance, landing or mooring fees, insurance, marketing and booking fees.
Cost per guest = hourly cost x hours / guests.
Break-even load factor = cost per trip / (price x seats).
Seasonal pricing and group offers must stay above cost.
Hourly cost 40,000 INR for a 1-hour trip with 8 seats is 5,000 INR per seat. At 6,000 INR a seat, break-even is 83 per cent full.
Build a cost sheet and break-even load factor.
Maths is correct and the currency is shown.
Environment and community
Evaluate
Tourism lasts only if neighbours and nature are protected.
Noise, wildlife disturbance, emissions and waste.
Fly or sail around nesting and breeding areas and keep minimum heights or distances.
Use local guides and suppliers; share some benefit with the community.
Publish your commitments.
The route avoids a nesting beach in spring and keeps above 300 m over houses. Neighbours receive a flight schedule.
List five environmental and community commitments with measures.
Each commitment has a number or rule.
Operations plan and guest care
Create
Bring it all together into a plan staff can follow.
Roles, schedule, records, training and spare parts.
Guest journey: booking, reminders, arrival, briefing, trip, thanks and feedback.
Complaints and refunds within a stated time.
Review each season.
The plan reaches an average guest score of 4.7 out of 5 in the first 20 trips and cuts late arrivals with a reminder message.
Write the operations plan and present it.
Plan includes roles, records, guest journey and a review date.
quiz: Who may operate?
Licensed operators and crew. (Covered in module 2: Licences, certificates and insurance. To pass that module: Every item has an authority, document number or practice placeholder and a date.)
Go/no-go factors?
Wind, visibility, waves or ceiling. (Covered in module 3: Weather rules and go/no-go decisions. To pass that module: Rules have limits, decision maker and guest message.)
Briefing items?
Equipment, exits, behaviour. (Covered in module 4: Briefing and equipment. To pass that module: Script covers equipment, exits, behaviour and emergency, and a peer can repeat it.)
Cost per guest?
Hourly cost x hours / guests. (Covered in module 6: Costs, price and break-even. To pass that module: Maths is correct and the currency is shown.)
Why drills?
Find weaknesses. (Covered in module 5: Emergency planning and drills. To pass that module: Plan has roles, contacts and drill results.)
Insurance for?
Passengers. (Covered in module 2: Licences, certificates and insurance. To pass that module: Every item has an authority, document number or practice placeholder and a date.)
Why check expiry?
Valid permits. (Covered in module 2: Licences, certificates and insurance. To pass that module: Every item has an authority, document number or practice placeholder and a date.)
Environment control?
Avoid nesting sites. (Covered in module 7: Environment and community. To pass that module: Each commitment has a number or rule.)
Cancel policy?
Refund. (Covered in module 8: Operations plan and guest care. To pass that module: Plan includes roles, records, guest journey and a review date.)
What are checks logged?
Equipment inspection. (Covered in module 4: Briefing and equipment. To pass that module: Script covers equipment, exits, behaviour and emergency, and a peer can repeat it.)
